description_block:
Jimoh Bola Akolo (Nigerian, 1934-2023)
Sleep 
inscribed '9' and bears a label inscribed 'J.B AKOLO' (verso)
oil on board
121.5 x 60cm (47 13/16 x 23 5/8in).

Provenance
The collection of Dennis Duerden (1929-2007);
A private collection, UK.

Sleep is an excellent example of the artists in 'designing a surface with shapes of color'(C. Okeke-Agulu, p. 126), a practise that enforces the view that Jimoh Bola Akolo is one of the most significant artists in Nigerian Modernism. The geometrical composition of this work could be said to derive from a brief period in the early 1960's when Akolo drew inspiration from the geometrically pattered facades of Hausa architecture common to Northern Nigeria. Through pallet and compositional construction, Akolo presents us with fragmented figures contrasted by the splatter of paint in the final touches of his process.

Jimoh Akolo was a founding member of the Zaria Art Society (1958-62), along with Yusuf Grillo, Bruce Onobrakpeya, and other art students at the Zaria branch of the Nigerian College of Arts, Science and Technology. This group, along with their peers in literature, theatre, music constituted a postcolonial modernist vanguard in Nigeria in the early 1960s. Convinced that a new art appropriate for Nigerian and African political independence must combine indigenous and western modernist aesthetics, forms and processes, this generation of artists set about creating spaces—such as the now-legendary journal Black Orpheus and the Mbari Writers and Artists Club, Ibadan—for the production and discourse of Nigerian and African modernism.

Bibliography
C.Okeke-Agulu, Postcolonial Modernism: Art and Decolonization in Twentieth-Century Nigeria, (Durham: Duke University Press, 2015)

The present work is akin to the Mobilization series created between around the millennium displaying the Hausa preparing for war on horseback. Prior to war, the horses assemble to mobilise themselves before embarking on combat. Jimoh Akolo built upon this idea while in Zaria city where riders would assemble during Sallah or other major celebrations like the Durbar.

The present work is expressionistic in application, closely cropped, and is characteristic to the artists erasure of details inline with the tension he achieves in composition between illusion, one-point perspective, and shallow scene via the red flat background. Indeed, this work epitomises Akolos applied intellectual skill with masterful creativity.

description_block:
Yusuf Adebayo Cameron Grillo (Nigerian, 1934-2021)
One Man Band 
bears a label inscribed 'ONE MAN BAND/ OIL ON BOARD/ by/ Y GRILLO/ 1967' (verso)
oil on board
117 x 74cm (46 1/16 x 29 1/8in).
(unframed)

Provenance
Acquired directly from the artist;
The collection of Mr Aldo Whistance Grant.

Exhibited
London, Commonwealth Institute Art Gallery, Contemporary Nigerian Art, (20th June - 21st July 1968), no. 64.

Painted in 1967, One Man Band was completed during Yusuf Grillo's rise to international acclaim and prominence. In this elongated and cubist form, Grillo is able to communicate a dignified elegant silhouette coherent in the geometric aesthetic he often used in his most iconic figurative paintings. Recognised for his dynamic and academically informed paintings, synthesising traditional Yoruba sculptural characteristics with his Western formal training, works such as the present lot embody his 'open text' approach in that they are an observation of his own surroundings. This ethos allowed a plethora of interpretations to be accessed from his works and morphologies enabling the audience to access and appreciate these works from various interpretations. 

As a founder of the Zaria art society, Yusuf Grillo is widely considered as one of the most influential figures in Nigerian Modernism. Alongside founders such as Jimoh Akolo and Bruce Onobrakpeya, as well as contemporaries in music, theatre, and literature, Akolo conceived that a new artistic development was to be born from Nigerian and African political independence. A key principal to the society was the concept of 'natural synthesis', as Grillo explained "You have to know who you are. You have to know your roots. Not because you are an artist, but for the simple reason that you are a person." ("Yusuf Grillo: An Interview," in P. Dike & P. Oyelola, (1998), p. 64.). It was the belief that to embed oneself into the culture which they are from and in which they currently exist was essential to one's artistic practice.

As evidence of his artistic and academic prowess, Grillo held the position as the Head of the Department of Art and Printing at Yaba College of Technology for more than 25 years. Beyond painting and education, Grillo's practises extended to those of architectural influence, whether that be sculpture, stain glasswork, and mosaic. Indeed, the provenance of this work includes Aldo Whistance Grant (Bill Grant), who was an architect for James Cubbit. Cubitt was an architect who specialised in churches and non-conformist chapels, architectural structures also relevant to Grillo given his commitment to designing stain glass windows. Indeed, the present works use of cool blues, violet, and green is reminiscent of the stained glass that Grillo's practise extended to. It could be argued that Grant's architectural eye was drawn to the hews and geometric aesthetic nature of the works. Grant selected this work in Grillo's studio between late 1967 and early 1968, only to be informed that it was to be included in an exhibition in London that year. Therefore, he was not able to take possession of the work later in 1968 on its return to Lagos.

The sensitivity of his brush strokes allow the audience to view a figure holding what appear to be a set of drums and what could be a soprillo saxophone. The figure is anonymous, the emphasis of his identity lying in his instruments, and indeed the title. Yusuf Grillo was an admirer of music, often incorporating musicians as subject matter, and rhythm in composition and brushstroke. It was of his opinion that the each artistic practise shared a commonality and a fluidity. Beyond this holistic approach, music played a core and nostalgic component to his heritage:

'I used to go close, watch and join the music, look at the dancers and join them too. They made a very, very strong impression, an indelible impression. And what interests me most is what the drummers do when they are not actually playing. That is, when they have an interval at which time they try to re-tune their instruments, that is, the drum skins, which they place over a small fire. They would get some rough paper together, light it and place the drum over it so that the skin would be taut. The fact is that when they have been drumming, the skin goes a little slack, so the sound is not what it should be. Hence, they do all that just to warm it and make it taut, to bring back the desired sound. These are some of the things in traditional drumming that interest me most.'(Professor Yusuf Grillo, 13th November 2005).

One Man Band not only demonstrates a development of heritage with a Nigerian modern artforms though the ethos of 'natural synthesis', but also displays Grillo's commitment to developing an 'open text' narrative synthesised with personal nostalgia. 

Bibliography
P. Dike & P. Oyelola, The Zaria Art Society, (Lagos, 1998), pp. 87-96.
P. Chike Dike and P. Oyelola (eds.), Master of Masters Yusuf Grillo: His Life and Works, (Nigeria: National Gallery of Art, 2006).
C.Okeke-Agulu, Postcolonial Modernism: Art and Decolonization in Twentieth-Century Nigeria, (Durham, 2015).

description_block:
Ladi Kwali (Nigerian, circa 1925-1984)
Water vessel 
stamped 'L.K.' (towards base)
unglazed terracotta
38 x 38 x 38cm (14 15/16 x 14 15/16 x 14 15/16in).

Provenance
Acquired by Janice Koenig Ross;
Bequeathed to a private US collection.

One of the very few Tuskegee demonstration pots known to exist, the present work is a rare and exceptional example of Ladi Kwali's practice. The absence of the traditional glaze finish makes this a particularly distinctive work, revealing the precision of Kwali's hand in the execution of her iconic sgraffito decoration.

Ladi Kwali began making pottery at the age of six, learning the traditional techniques practised by women in her Gwari community from her aunt. Her pottery would attract the admiration of the Emir of Abuja, an early collector of her work. In 1950, she was further regarded with great esteem by Michael Cardew who encountered her upon his research tour of Abuja in 1950 after his recruitment by the Nigerian colonial government as Pottery Officer in the department of Commerce and Industry. The following year, he would invite Ladi Kwali to join the Abuja Pottery Training Centre. Already an established potter with her own shop in the nearby town of Minna, Kwali was the first woman to join the training centre in 1954. Design historian Tanya Harrod described Kwali's process in the following: 

"She starts by punching into a solid cylinder of clay, pulling up the sides, adding rough coils of clay, walking round and round the pot, scraping and thinning the pot's wall while the whole thing sways outrageously. The shape is then bellied out and an elegant rim created by manipulating a piece of cloth or leather. The end result has perfect symmetry and classical rightness. Ladi Kwali was a past mistress of this and she was also peculiarly imaginative about decorating, always ready to try new ideas. To awed outsiders she appeared to go into a trance-like state as she incised outlines and cross-hatching with a knife-like tool, working her way round the pot without any preliminary setting out." 

In mid-March 1972, Ladi Kwali, together with fellow potter Clement Kofi Athey and Michael Cardew, embarked on a demonstration tour of the United States and Canada, beginning in Chattanooga, Tennessee, and lasting approximately two and a half months. The demonstrations followed a collaborative format: Kofi prepared the clay, Cardew lectured and presented slides, yet the central event was Kwali's construction of a hand-built pot, demonstrating the traditional techniques she had learned in Nigeria. 

Two demonstration pots were created at the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1972, one of which is the present lot. There, Kwali demonstrated her traditional Gbagyi hand-coiling technique, working progressively around the vessel and adding successive coils to build its height and breadth. The pot was then decorated with her characteristic zoomorphic sgraffito imagery, combining a distinctive personal vocabulary with traditional Gwari techniques.

This demonstration tour grew Kwali's fame internationally following her award of an MBE in 1962 and an honorary doctorate from Ahmadu Bello University in Zaria. Since the tour, Ladi Kwali's image is used on the 20 Naira Nigerian bank note since 1977 and received the Officer of the Order of the Niger (OON) in 1981, emphasising her importance to the country. Through this exposure, acknowledgments, and a global respect for her practice, Kwali's work continues to influence a number of next generation of potters and artists such as Magdalene Odundo.

The present work thus brings together the traditional methods of Gwari pottery with the new contexts in which Kwali's work was presented internationally. Its unglazed surface is particularly revealing, allowing the incised decoration to be appreciated as the direct record of Kwali's hand and demonstrating the remarkable control that distinguished her work.

Janice Koenig Ross (1926-2020) was a Professor of Art Tuskegee Institute from 1968 to 1991. She arranged the visit of Michael Cardew and Ladi Kwali to Tuskegee during their US tour of 1972 and the pair lodged with Janice for several days during their stay.

Bibliography
John Edgeler, Michael Cardew and stoneware, continuity and change, (Winchcombe: Cotswolds living Publications, 2008)
C. Benfey, 'Michael Cardew: The Potter as Great Modern Artist', New Republic, (3 June, 2013).
Michael Cardew, Pioneer Pottery, (London: Longman Publishing Group, 1969), pp, 104-105.
Susan Vogel, Ladi Kwali, Michael Cardew and a Tangled Story of African Studio Pottery, ed, Kerstin Pinther, Alexandra Weigand, Flow of forms/Forms of flow, Design Histories between Africa and Europe, (Germany: Transcript publishing, 2018).

description_block:
Asibi Ido (Nigerian, c. 1940-1984)
Water Vessel 
stamped 'AI' (twice to base) and 'Abuja' [in Arabic] (base)
glazed stoneware
36 x 36 x 36cm (14 3/16 x 14 3/16 x 14 3/16in).

Provenance
A private UK collection.

Documented by Edgeler as joining the Training Centre in 1963, Asibi Ido is classed, along with the other female potters such as Ladi Kwali, Kande Ushafa, and Lami Toto, as one of the most prominent potter's of the centre. This was evident when one of her pots was presented to President Azikiwe when he visited the centre.

The present lot embodies key elements of Abuja pottery, from the Abuja Jun glazing in a wonderfully high-fired finish, to the zoomorphic and plant representation etchings that encompass the present work across the drum of the vessel. Synthesizing the adapted shape from Gwari traditional forms of water vessels, to the female potters modern and more decorative adaptation, the present work is a prime example of modern Abuja pottery.

Bibliography
John Edgeler, Michael Cardew and stoneware, continuity and change, (Winchcombe: Cotswolds living Publications, 2008).

El Anatsui (Ghanaian, born 1944)
Ancestors Gaze 
signed and dated 'EL/95' (panel 17)
wood roots, carved and painted in tempera with fabrics
200 x 110 x 15cm (78 3/4 x 43 5/16 x 5 7/8in).

The present work belongs to the Ancestor series, a group of figurative sculptures the artist executed in 1995. One of the larger pieces, titled The Ancestors Converged Again, is now in the collection of the Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of African Art, Washington. 

The Ancestor works featured in El Anatsui's 1995 show at the October Gallery in London, Sculptures and Reliefs, one of his first solo exhibitions outside of Africa. He had been creating wall reliefs from carved wooden planks since the early 1980s. The sculptures became increasingly complex and sophisticated over the next decade, reaching a peak in the mid 90s. The current lot is composed from twenty-one wooden posts and branches cut from a variety of trees. Each pole has been carved with a face, painted, and adorned with material to represent the kente cloth of traditional Ghanaian dress.

Bibliography

description_block:
Ablade Glover (Ghanaian, born 1934)
Market Scene 
signed and dated 'Glo/ 14' (lower right)
oil on canvas
101.5 x 151.5cm (39 15/16 x 59 5/8in).

Provenance
Acquired directly from the artist in 2016;
A private collection, UK.

Professor Ablade Glover was trained in Ghana, Britain and United States. He has accumulated numerous distinctions which demonstrate his importance as an artist and enthusiastic educator on the national and international art scene. It is generally contested that contemporary Ghanaian art developed in response to the introduction of Western concepts at the start of the nineteenth century. As this genre of art has developed, an aesthetic acculturation of complex African representations and inspirations fused with western modes of artistic expression, has emerged. Professor Ablade Glover follows the first generation of Ghanaian artists, post-independence, who explored African urban subjects in a more realistic vein, linking the state of Ghana to a mythological past of African tradition.

Market places, lorry parks, shanty towns and other urban spaces, crowded with ordinary people are regular themes explored by Glover. His artworks demonstrate the natural connection of the traditional African and modern Western styles. Glover's use of colour and the textural qualities in his works, call to mind the brightly-coloured and textured Ghanaian fabrics and textiles. The paint is applied boldly as thick impasto, worked by deft strokes of the palette knife into a type of thick carpet of glowing light and shade. Market Scene is both an abstract epiphany of colour and a detailed rendition of reality.

Bibliography
J.Castellote, Contemporary Nigerian Art in Lagos Private Collections,(Ibadan, 2012), pp.14 & 89

description_block:
Uzo Egonu (Nigerian, 1931-1996)
Will Knowledge Safeguard Freedom I 
signed and dated 'Uzo Egonu 1984-85' (lower right), bears inscription on stretcher "Will Knowledge Safeguard Freedom 1" (verso)
oil on canvas
188 x 295cm (74 x 116 1/8in).

Provenance
The collection of the artist;
A private collection, UK.

The second version of this work is illustrated in Olu Oguibe's book Uzo Egonu: An African Artist in the West. Both paintings are part of a series that Uzo Egonu embarked upon between the years of 1985 to 1988, the same period in which he developed his study of the 'Stateless People' series. Instead of focusing on the melancholic elements of social existence, Will Knowledge Safeguard Freedom I interrogates instead the power and knowledge of unity. In these specific paintings Egonu observes 'the ways in which scientific and technological advancement determine the fate and place of races, and the destiny of humankind'(p. 138). Egonu held an anxious preoccupation with the seemingly static attitude towards progress in Africa, demonstrated by the failed architectural, industrialisation, and development of experimental state-buildings across the continent, which was evidence, he felt, of continued repression. 

Greatly inspired by Japan's own historical technological advancement, Egonu is quoted in 1986 emphasising his philosophy that knowledge equates to power:

"My study of Japanese history helped me a lot in my art. I do not mean Japanese art, but Japanese studies of Western Science and technology and eventual industrialisation. Had Japan failed or ignored to acquaint herself with science and technology, she would have ended up as a Russian colony and could not have withstood the Russian Navy's onslaught last century, let alone defeat it. (Egonu, Unpublished Paper, 1986, in O.Oguibe, p. 139.).

Prompts, motifs, and metaphors are not unfamiliar additions made by the artist to his work in order to guide the viewer and display the intent with his work. To the upper left quadrant it is written "Is laziness = a bowl in hand + contempt?" and "Not until we create our own paradise" to the centre left. To the upper right; "Is Knowledge a fortification against ignorance and prejudice?". These lyrical slogans cut through the geometric forms of interlocked figures and industrial motifs. The words are one with the imagery, bolstering the viewers connection with the intensity of Egonu's thoughts, emotions, and aspirations. 

Like the incorporation of slogans, the ladder is also a consistent trope throughout this series of works. This imagery is used to convey the idea of ascent or descent, in other painting sometimes taking the form of a staircase. The ladder or staircase motif is present on other works such as A New Lease of Life (Third)(1989), a non-figurative, still life, self portrait of the artist following a period of physical blindness; the staircase symbolising his development and new world view, and for Egonu, physical sight.

What is intriguing and compelling in the depiction of the figures is the addition of blindfolds over their eyes, perhaps representing the blind faith and labour without immediate reward prior to a result of discovery, or the anticipation of knowledge. The blindfolded figures appear to hold books and gaze downwards. Some figures are compositionally cornered off by chains and bars to the lower right quadrant of the work. In line with this theory of the process from ignorance to knowledge, the central figure holding the ladder with outstretched arms does not wear a blindfold, personified with a simplistic minimalistic profile, contributes to this insinuation of enlightenment. Executed in hews of yellow illuminated from the rust and blue palette of the crowd, the contrast of these figures enforces this idea of escaping the bonds of ignorance and repression. 

'Effort and the quest for discovery, the artist argues through his imagery, are the keys to advancement and self-improvment for all humanity.' (O.Oguibe, p. 143).

Indeed the purpose of this painting is to draw attention to the lessons that can be learnt from universal history for the advancement and progression of the human race. Egonu's focus in this motive is not so much on oppression or failure as it is success and liberation. Works such as Will Knowledge Safeguard Freedom I is executed to display an incentive for education and motivation to develop and prosper.

Bibliography
 Olu Oguibe's, Uzo Egonu: An African Artist in the West, (London: Kala Press, 1995), pp. 137-146.

description_block:
Uzo Egonu (Nigerian, 1931-1996)
Kwame Nkrumah 
signed and dated 'Egonu/62' (lower right); bears a label numbered '21' (verso)
oil on canvas
167 x 122cm (65 3/4 x 48 1/16in).

Provenance
Sotheby's, Modern and Contemporary African Art, (May 2017), Lot 49;
A private collection.

1962 marked the first year of what Egonu described as 'the Bridge' in his work that would last until 1965. These were the formative years that saw a break from his focus of nostalgia in his work, in a move towards his abstracted pieces. This work can therefore be viewed as one of his last nostalgic pieces, stooped in traditional artforms that would however continue to inform the content and ethos of the works that would make his a pioneer of contemporary Nigerian painting. 

Nationalist pride sustained Egonu's private vow to devise a form of induvial cultural nationalism and to manifest this in his work. Although his physical contacts with home were not particularly strong and numerous, he followed events closely, and thus remained part of both the euphoria of the period, if guardedly so, and the concrete movement towards political and cultural redefinition in the country. (O. Oguibe, p.26).

The present work is an exquisite example of this, depicting the first President of Ghana since independence from colonial rule in 1957, Kwame Nkrumah. 

Egonu embarked on Kwame Nkrumah by beginning with neo-classical style sketches, framing him as an almost transcendent being, perhaps inspired by the politicians cult name Osagyefo (Great Teacher). Egonu was admitted an audience with the Nkrumah in 1961 on a visit to London which enabled him to fulfil life sketches for the present resultant painting.

Bibliography
O. Oguibe, Uzo Egonu: An African Artist in the West, (Kala, London: 1995).

Self Portrait 
inscribed "Self Portrait" (lower left), signed and dated "Akinola Lasekan 1955" (lower right); inscribed 'SELF-PORTRAIT/ 1955', '50', and bears a 'United Africa Company' stamp (verso)

52 x 42cm (20 1/2 x 16 9/16in).

Provenance

Exhibited

Literature
Terra Kulture Gallery, 'Akinola Lasekan: His Life, Works and Contributions to the Development of Contemporary Nigerian Art., (2012), p. 13, (illustrated).

Akinola Lasekan was a pioneering Nigerian painter, illustrator, cartoonist and art educator, whose career developed during the late colonial and early postcolonial periods. Born in Owo, southwestern Nigeria, Lasekan was largely self-trained before travelling to England in 1945, where he studied fine art at the Normal Training School of Art, now known as the Royal College of Art, in 1937 before studying at the Washington School of Art in the USA two years later. In 1940, Lasekan founded the Lash Studio Correspondence School which offered training in areas including book illustration, commercial art, and landscape and figurative drawing, reflecting Lasekan's commitment to making formal artistic education accessible beyond the established art schools.

This rare self-portrait exemplifies Lasekan's artistic flare, precision in both palette and application and naturalism. The work represents the artist at a period when his activities as painter, illustrator and educator were closely interconnected. Lasekan's advocacy of naturalistic drawing and portraiture formed an important part of his teaching practice and influenced subsequent generations of Nigerian artists.

Prince Twins Seven-Seven was born in Ijara, northern Nigeria, to the royal family of Osuntoki in 1944. He changed his birthname, Olaniyi Osuntoki, to signify his status as the sole survivor of his parents' seven sets of twins. He believed he was an 'abiku', a 'child born to die'. In Yoruba culture, abiku are thought to possess special gifts as a result of their connection to the spirit world.

Through his artwork, Twins creates a world with ties to Yoruba oral traditions, myths, religion and his own personal experiences. He has developed a technique known as sculpture painting, in which he raises the foreground of a painting to create a low relief. 

Prince Twins Seven-Seven shot to international fame in 2005 when the President of Nigeria, Olusegun Obasanjo, appointed him one of UNESCO's Artists for Peace.

Elias Sime (Ethiopian, born 1968)
"Tightrope 7", 2009-14 
mixed media and reclaimed components
260 x 993cm (102 3/8 x 390 15/16in).

Provenance
Acquired from the James Cohan Gallery, NYC, 2017;
A UK corporate collection.

Exhibited
New York, James Cohan Gallery, Elias Sime, (September-October 2015).

The present work was exhibited in Elias Sime's debut solo exhibition at James Cohan Gallery in 2015, alongside a closely related work exhibited at the Alliance Ethio-Française. Composed of found and collected materials acquired predominantly from Menalesh Tera (meaning "What do you have?"), a section of the Addis Ababa market, the work brings together an accumulation of electrical and everyday objects, meticulously arranged and adhered to individual, interlocking backing boards.

The present work is composed primarily of electrical components, interspersed with disparate materials as scraps of tin, pencils and old toys. Each individual element has been carefully selected, positioned and amalgamated into a meticulously constructed tapestry of accumulated matter. Viewed from a distance, the dense assemblage resolves into sweeping circular and diagonal movements that animate the surface and create a striking sense of rhythm.

The present work forms part of Sime's Tightrope series that began in 2013 and initially developed from more than fifteen years of collecting electrical components and related materials. The earliest works in the series were subsequently exhibited in Addis Ababa at the British Council, the Goethe-Institut, the Instituto Italiano di Cultura and the Alliance Ethio-Française. Across the series, Sime transforms remnants of technological consumption into densely layered compositions that consider the increasingly intimate relationship between human beings and technology.

Tightrope 7 particularly explores the erosion of direct human connection in an increasingly technologically mediated world. As Sime has commented:

"There needs to be a space between us and our machines. They have practically become parts of our bodies. Without criticizing or dismissing these machines, we should stop and create a distance from them for the laughter and pleasure of face-to-face humanity." (E.Sime, Bomb, 2019).

As Tracy L. Adler observes, Sime's practice is "informed by a consideration of the profound impact technology has had in shaping human consciousness and our relationship with the environment."(T. Alder, 2019, p. 52.)

Monumental in scale and materially abrasive in appearance, the work confronts the viewer with the physical consequences of mass production and technological consumption, transforming discarded objects into a meditation on the systems of production, connection and obsolescence that underpin contemporary life.

Created in relation to the Mozart's opera The Magic Flute, William Kentridge executed this series Magic Flute: Dove (States I-X) between 2006 and 2007. Premiering in 2005, Kentridge produced a production of the opera at the Théâtre Royal de la Monnaie in Brussels that would tour in France, Italy, the United States, and end in South Africa in 2007. While a central figure of the opera is a bird catcher, the philosophy of what the bird represented held significance to Kentridge. In conversation with Brownyn Law-Viljoen in a 2007 interview, a link to the concepts of consciousness by William James, a late nineteenth and early twentieth century philosopher and proto-psychologist who believed language could be characterised in the same way as a bird's life is made up of altered states, between stillness and movement. Kentridge argued:

"It is not as if there is simply the bird flying and that is thought. Thought may follow one particular path, but there are all other paths not taken, and all other paths still being thought through, or not yet though of, the language can latch on to at different stages and goes on. Which is why I have not talked of a "stream of consciousness" that is solitary but diffuse, but rather a "highway of consciousness" where you have a channel but many different lanes and different things moving in different lanes, overtaking, stopping, leaving the highway." 

"In so far as the polemic of the opera goes: it is about a messy, mixed state of things, between darkness and enlightenment."(Kentridge, p. 23.)

The present work was likely included in the 1962 Hampton Institute that toured America through USA Tour in 1950 based on artworks from the Harmon Foundation. This tour extended through the Howard University, Boston, Vasser College, Syracuse University, Bennington College, and the Fisk University.

Enwonwu's masterful use of light and dark, depth, perspective, drama and dynamism of this piece. This piece possesses a particular narrative in its heavy use of light and texture as a focal point of the work. Enwonwu has used variations of paint application, thinning his paint in some areas while others are layered in thick impasto.

An abstract use of red to the centre of the piece is a demonstration of Enwonwus creative flare, but also his acute understanding of colour. Unique its rare varied application, yet coherent with some of Benedict Enwonwus most celebrated and dynamic works such as Marianne, Enwonwus masterful juxtaposition of colour is ever-present through his portraits, landscapes, and forest-scapes. The red and green pigmentation contrast each other, holding the viewers gaze. Passages of red were not an unusual technique used by the artist as this method was employed in some of the artists most championed portraits such as Portrait of Marianne (1972) and My Mama at 80 (1973). This colour technicality trope could be argued as inspired by the impressionist Paul Cézanne, 'Cézanne was a bad technician but he is among the greatest of the Impressionists' (Enwonwu quoted in S. Ogbechie, 2008: p. 107). However, what is unusual is the techniques employment here in a woodland scene.

Trees at Nekede near Oweri, was a common site that Enwonwu visited, evidently holding a special place personally to Enwonwu. Another similar work, Nekede Village Market Owerri (1949) exhibited at Galerie Apollinaire in 1950, demonstrates the artists commitment to the area.

P. Chike Dike and Pat Oyelola describe 1962, the year Uche Okeke spent in Germany under a federal scholarship, as perhaps the most productive period of his career. Attached to the Franz Mayer studio in Munich, Okeke encountered a new cultural and artistic environment that expanded the scope of his practice. As Dike and Oyelola observe, his pen-and-ink drawings gave way to the powerful Munich Suite, which marked an expressive high point in his exploration of Uli: "The German experience gave a certain cosmopolitan openness to Okeke's themes," with subjects ranging from "the madmen and the curly haired girls of Munich" to Birds in Flight and Time Bird, suggesting, in their words, "a Brancusi consciousness, perhaps." (P. Chike Dike, Pat Oyelola, p. 132.)

Created in 1962, Head of a Girl is a compelling example of this pivotal Munich period. Executed in gouache on paper, the work reveals Okeke's increasingly assured synthesis of Igbo Uli aesthetics and the formal experimentation of European modernism. Its minimalistic, fluid composition transforms the human head into an arrangement of sinuous lines and rhythmic curves, demonstrating the expressive possibilities Okeke found in the visual language of Uli.

"The importance of Uche Okeke lies in his recognition of the possibilities of Uli as a design resource for enriching modern art and, together with Nigeria's other innovators, of providing us with real "20th Century African Art"". (Frank Aig-Imoukhuede, Foreword of 'Uche Okeke: 60th Birthday Anniversary Retrospective Exhibition', p.4.)

Sam Joseph Ntiro (Tanzanian, 1923-1993)
At the pool 
signed 'S. J Ntiro' (lower right); bears a label inscribed 'At the Pool, Sam Joseph Ntiro, Kilimanjaro 1956' (verso)

Exhibited
Merton D. Simpson Gallery, NYC, May 1960.

Literature
Mario Pissarra, 'Re/writing Sam J Ntiro: Challenges of framing in the excavation of a 'lost' pioneer', Tird Text Africa, Vol. 4, (2015), p. 40. (illustrated).

Sam Joseph Ntiro is widely recognised today as a pioneering Tanzanian artist, diplomat, and educator. Born in the Kilimanjaro region in the North-West of Tanzania, in a village called Ndereny, he studied at the Makerere College of the University of East Africa. He then studied Art and Education at the University of London before completing a postgraduate degree at the Slade School of Fine Art. Continuing his passion for artistic education, he developed the Department of Music, Arts and Culture at the University of Dar es Salaam where he also served as a Lecturer. Ntiro also served as chairman of the Tanzania Arts society and the Tanzania Crafts Council. His leadership roles were frequent and extensive. In his political career, he served as the First East African High Commissioner of Saint James in London and as the Ambassador to Ireland from the Tanganyika Territory during the years of independence from 1961, serving until 1964. Ntiro also served as the Commissioner of Culture for the Government of the United Republic of Tanzania from 1967 to 1973. It was during this time that he also researched extensively across America in Fine Art and African studies at universities in New Orleans, Louisiana, and Wisconsin.

Sam Joseph Ntiro's extensive and impressive career is reflected in his global recognition. The first artist from East Africa to hold a solo exhibition at a gallery in New York, the Merton D. Simpson gallery in 1960, of which this present lot was included, saw his career escalate and break boundaries for other African artists to follow. This exhibition attracted the attention of the MoMA in New York who would purcahse Men Taking Banana Beer to Bride by Night (1956). It was this acquisition from this same exhibition that made Sam Ntiro the first modern African artist to have one of his works purchased by MoMA in New York.

Ntiro was committed to depicting scenes inspired by his memory of the Chagga country having not lived in Tanzania since 1944, twelve years prior to this works completion. While he had visited, a Ugandan colonial officer supporting Ntiro's application to the Slade wrote in 1951, "He lives far away from his own people and country." The present work is an exemplary example of Ntiro's balance between reality and imagined worlds. The layered treatment in composition is highlighted by the artists tendency to begin with a lighter palette, ultimately layering with darker heus. This creates a sense of mysticism that is further enforced by the seeming disregard for realistic depictions of scale. The figures become one with nature for a unified rhythmic scene. Professor George Kyeyune noted on works such as these:

"Ntiro's painting offers many such surprises: it depicts nature but it resists the temptation of imitating it. It invents its own mixture of fantasy and reality, and allows them to share the same territorial space without undermining the vitality of the picture." (G. Kyeyune, p. 140.)

Contextually, this work is situated within an exhibition that would cement Sam J Ntiro's position on the global stage. An impressive businessman and artist in his own right, his almost surreal yet deeply personal works are are a testament to the love of his country and his creative genius.

description_block:
Alexis Preller (South African, 1911-1975)
Musical Troupe from All Africa 
signed and dated 'Preller '56' (lower right)
oil on canvas 
25.5 x 78.5cm (10 1/16 x 30 7/8in).

Provenance
A private collection, US.

Painted in 1956, only a year after the completion of his monumental triptych All Africa (1953–55), the present work dates from a particularly fertile moment in Preller's career. Commissioned for the Receiver of Revenue building in Johannesburg, All Africa brought together many of the sources that had occupied the artist during the preceding years, combining African sculptural traditions with the hieratic conventions of ancient Egyptian art and impressions gathered during his travels through Italy and Egypt in 1953.

The group of musicians in the present work finds a striking parallel in the ceremonial procession running across the lower register of the central panel of All Africa. There, an enthroned figure playing an elongated drum is surrounded by musicians carrying horns, drums and stringed instruments. Their stylised forms, ceremonial dress and rhythmic arrangement reflect Preller's interest in the courtly imagery of the historic Kingdom of Benin, whose sculpture and relief traditions became an important part of his visual vocabulary during this period.

Preller continued to revisit and transform this imagery after the completion of the mural. A particularly revealing comparison is The Herald (1955), exhibited at the Lidchi Gallery in Johannesburg in March 1956. Its horn-playing figure has been directly associated with the procession in All Africa, as though a single character from the monumental composition had been isolated and given an independent pictorial life.

The present work appears to develop this idea further. Here, the musicians are brought together into a tighter, more intimate group, transforming the processional rhythm of All Africa into a self-contained composition. Removed from the monumental setting of the triptych, they nevertheless retain the ceremonial and hieratic quality that characterises Preller's work of the mid-1950s.

Preller's use of such imagery was not intended as the literal representation of a particular culture. Elements drawn from Benin, ancient Egypt and elsewhere were absorbed and reimagined within his own visual mythology. In the present work, music and ceremony become part of that imagined world: rooted in identifiable African sources, yet transformed into something distinctly Preller's own.

Bibliography
Esmé Berman and Karel Nel, Alexis Preller: Africa, the Sun and Shadows, Johannesburg, Shelf Publishing, 2009.

description_block:
Alexis Preller (South African, 1911-1975)
Mapogga Women 
signed and dated 'Preller 51' (lower left)
oil on canvas laid on board
24.7 x 38.5cm (9 3/4 x 15 3/16in).

Preller first encountered the people he called the 'Mapogga' (a term devised by the Boer settlers to name the Ndzundza group of the Southern Ndebele people) in 1935 on a sketching trip north of Pretoria. He came across a group of Ndebele women working in the fields and followed them to their village. Enraptured by the indigenous dress of the women, Preller embarked upon a career-long artistic project to capture his perception of the 'Mapogga' culture. While the first work on the 'Mapogga' theme was exhibited in 1936, the present work marks Preller's particular interest in the Ndebele women which he began to pursue with renewed vigour in the early 1950s. 

In his treatment of the theme, Preller was not motivated to produce anthropological studies of the indigenous communities he encountered in South Africa. Crucially, his depictions of the Ndebele women (who served as his greatest source of inspiration) were rather shaped by his desire to formulate an iconic symbol of the essence of Africa – a distinctly modernist enterprise out of step with contemporary attitudes. His figures are consequently highly stylised with elongated limbs, and small ovoid heads. 

The present work marks an eager revisit into the 'Mapogga' as content for Preller, since his first experiment with theme in 1935. In the present work, the arms, necks, and ankles of the women are encircled with the rings typically worn by the Ndebele and their clothing is reimagined as geometric forms that enshroud the figures. Through a process of formal simplification, Preller transforms the matriarchs into icons 'through which I can convey what Africa means to me' (Preller quoted in E. Berman and K. Nel, 2009a: p. 146).

Preller conceived of his depiction of the 'Mapogga' people in relation to both his own situated experience and the avant-garde in Western art history. He described his painterly project as a means 'to identify myself with my age and place: Africa and the Twentieth Century' (Preller quoted in Esmé Berman and Karel Nel, 2009b: p. ix). The artist had left for England in 1934 where he studied for a year at the Westminster School of Art. In 1937 he continued his studies at the Académie de la Grande Chaumière in Paris. Here, he engaged with the paintings of French Post-Impressionists including Paul Gaugin and Vincent van Gogh, along with the work of twentieth-century modernists including Picasso whose paintings dominated the city's galleries in the 1930s. The stylisation of the figures in Preller's 'Mapogga' works resound with references to this European modernism along with the surrealist aesthetic of the Italian artist, Giorgio de Chirico.

Esmé Berman and Karel Nel, A Visual Biography. Alexis Preller: Africa, the Sun and Shadows, (Saxonwold, Johannesburg, 2009a).

Anton van Wouw (South African, 1862-1945)
Die Noitje van die Onderveld (The maiden of the lower-veld) 
signed, inscribed and dated "Anton van Wouw, 1907, SA Joh-burg', 'Transvaal Rustenburg syn distrikt' and bears Foundry Inscription 'G. Nisini fuse Roma'
bronze
42.5 x 15 x 15cm (16 3/4 x 5 7/8 x 5 7/8in.)

Literature
ML du Toit, Suid Afrikaanse Kunstenaars: Anton van Wouw. Nationale Pers. Pub 1933, another cast, ill., plate 5. 
Cohen, MJ., Anton van Wouw: Sculptor of South African Life, Johannesburg: Radford, Adlington, pb., 1938, another cast ill., pg., 25.

Anton van Wouw's "Die Noitjie van die Onderveld" is an important sculpture that reflects the cultural identity and values associated with Afrikaner society in the early 20th century. The young girl's traditional clothing, modest posture and quiet expression suggest ideals of innocence, femininity and humility that were strongly associated with the Afrikaner community, it represents the notion of the Afrikaner "volksmoeder", representing the idealised Afrikaner woman and her role in preserving family, culture and heritage.

From 1906 to 1916 John Purves worked in South Africa, becoming Professor of English at the Transvaal Technical Institute in Johannesburg and later at Transvaal University College, Pretoria.

Purves and van Wouw were both part of Pretoria's cultural world when the Transvaal University College (TUC) was being established. Purves was one of the original four professors when the TUC's Pretoria campus opened in 1908 and later became its first honorary librarian. Significantly, five of Van Wouw's bronzes were included in the exhibition at the TUC Pretoria in November 1910.

Anyanwu 
signed and dated 'BEN ENWONWU 58' (front lower centre of figure)

(excluding base)

Provenance

A private Nigerian collection.

In the present work's debut to auction, this rendition of Anyanwu stands as one of the most culturally significant works produced by the great Nigerian modernist Ben Enwonwu. Other large scale versions of Anyanwu such as the present lot are held in the collections of National Museum of Lagos (commissioned by Kenneth Murray), The United Nations, and the National Museum of Zimbabwe in Harare.

The superficial and esoteric meaning of the title work 'Anyanwu' are differentiated by Mcphilips Nwachukwu. From a global observation 'Anyanwu' is understood as a reflection of the 'history and political transformation' while esoterically, this theme utilised by Enwonwu expresses divinity and spirituality as expressed by the artist himself:

"My aim was to symbolise our rising nation. I have tried to combine material, crafts, and traditions, to express a conception that is based on womanhood – woman, the mother and nourisher of man. In our rising nation, I see the forces embodied in womanhood; the beginning, and then, the development and flowering into the fullest stature of a nation – a people! This sculpture is spiritual in conception, rhythmical in movement, and three dimensional in its architectural setting – these qualities are characteristic of the sculpture of my ancestors."(B. Enwonwu, 1957).

The pronounced curvature of the figure's lower body accords the statue's sense of distilled movement, her elongated form and distinct lines emphasise her measured poise and deliberate elegance. Regal in gold, scale, and elegance, the grandeur of the present work reflects the essence Enwonwu strove to emulate. These tropes of the elongated female form are not uncommon to Enwonwu's practice. Furthermore, Enwonwu's focus on womanhood as a central theme has maintained significant and central importance throughout the artists oeuvre. Indeed, the artist's words clearly express his belief that 'Anyanwu' was a visual manifestation of the new Nigeria, culturally-confident and proud of her heritage and history. It was fitting that in 1966, five years after Nigeria gained its independence from the United Kingdom in October 1960, that another version of Anyanwu was presented at the United Nations Headquarters in New York.

In reference to the date of the work's completion, two years before Nigerian independence from colonial rule, 1958 was a pivotal year for the trajectory of the artists career and also that of Nigerian Modernism, as it also the year that the Zaria art society was formed. Whilst Enwonwu himself was not included in the formation of the society, this only contributes to the sense of national hope and pride that was evidently present in the social, cultural, and political landscape. Moreover, this work was created at a personally pivotal time for Ben Enwonwu following his commission to complete a statue of HM Queen Elizabeth II a year prior to the creation of the present work, Anyanwu.

Victor Butler is a self-taught Ghanaian painter whose work explores the shifting relationship between the human figure and its surroundings. His compositions are built through concealment and transformation: faces emerge from fields of colour, bodies dissolve into landscape, and forms change depending on how they are read. This ambiguity is central to Butler's practice, allowing a single image to carry several forms at once.
With a background in medicine, technology and design, Butler came to painting outside a conventional artistic education. His work draws particularly on the natural world and African histories and narratives, bringing them into images that move between observation and imagination.

His works have been exhibited in Canada, England, France, Nigeria and the United States. In 2024, the Nubuke Foundation in Accra presented Heart Sensing, a retrospective of his work. His first solo exhibition in Nigeria, Nuance, was held in Lagos in 2018.

description_block:
David Goldblatt (South African, 1930-2018)
The farmer's son with his nursemaid, on the farm in Heimweeberg, near Nietverdiend in the Marico Bushveld. Transvaal (North-West Province) 
signed and dated 'David Goldblatt/ 1964' (verso); bears a descriptive label (verso)

image size 40.5 x 59.5cm (15 15/16 x 23 7/16in).
sheet size: 41 x 60cm (16 1/8 x 23 5/8in).

As part of his his seminal series, Some Afrikaners (1961-68), David Goldblatt produced The farmer's son with his nursemaid, on the farm in Heimweeberg, near Nietverdiend in the Marico Bushveld. Transvaal (North-West Province), a photograph that would become one of his most famous photographs. During this period, Goldblatt shot purely in black and white to emphasise and focus on the content he was capturing. 

Taken in 1964, in the rural area of Heimweeberg, the present photograph is a striking display of the true nature of the human race and historical circumstances that enforced the socio-politics of the time. The hateful racial and economic divides of Apartheid that were the contextual reality of South Africa are challenged in this deeply intimate shot. Moreover, this is a work of contradiction. The affection expressed between the two individuals in this photograph (the boy with his hands on her shoulders, she holding his ankle) contrasts the context in which they are brought together. Labelled the boys 'nursemaid', this portrait emphasises that the woman is a domestic worker for the family. The underlying class and racial divides separating the two seem blissfully obliterated in this unified piece.

Bibliography
Judy Ditner, et al. "David Goldblatt: No Ulterior Motive," eds. Judy Ditner, Leslie M. Wilson, and Matthew S. Witkovsky, pl. 3, p. 13 (New Haven: Yale University Press, 2023).
Michael Stevenson

Deborah Margaret Bell (South African, born 1957)

(this work is accompanied by a description of the piece)

The accompanying description to this work reads:

Journey Home IV
This piece is part of a series, which forms a procession of horse and rider figures. These figures, based on fragments from African sculpture, float in an indeterminate space—which although originally influenced by the arrangements of such artefacts in museum cases—now evolve an infinite spiritual space. The horse and rider figures are reminiscent of the journeyings of the Magi. They suggest a unity of body and soul, an embodiment of the spirit's journey—the Journey Home.
Deborah Bell 2000

This work belongs to a series of works Bell executed between 1999 and 2000 entitled The Journey Home. The artist was inspired by a sentence she came across in a collection of writings by Max Beckmann, On my Painting:

"I am seeking for a bridge which leads from the visible to the invisible, like the famous cabalist who once said, 'If you wish to get hold of the invisible you must penetrate as deeply as possible into the visible'." (Beckmann 1988, p. 12)

Beckmann's words resonated with Bell and her own quest for the 'Self'. She too seeks to 'penetrate' the material world and unearth the hidden truths through making art. For her, the creative process is 'the journey home', the route to truth and meaning.

Bibliography
P. Stein, Deborah Bell, (Johannesburg, 2004), pp. 7-11.
Max Beckmann, On my Painting, ed. George Scrivani, (Hanuman Books, 1988).

Robert Griffiths Hodgins (South African, 1920-2010)

signed, titled and dated 'Robert Hodgins/ Prison Games/ o/c 2005/6' and bears a label with the lot description and inscribed '24.' (verso) 
oil on canvas 
90 x 120cm (35 7/16 x 47 1/4in).

This painting was executed in 2005 and refers to the interrogation tactics used on prisoners detained at Guantanamo Bay. Earlier in the year, the case of Detainee 063 made the cover of TIME magazine.

TIME magazine had obtained the 84-page secret interrogation log of Detainee 063. Not intended for public release, the leaked document provided the first window into the internal workings of the classified Gitmo interrogations since the detention camp opened. It spanned 50 days over the winter of 2002-3, during which 16 additional interrogation techniques were approved by the US Defense Secretary.

The log did not indicate how successful these additional measures were in obtaining intelligence. The case fuelled international debate about whether such techniques were an abuse of detainees' rights.

Hodgins depicts a slumped anonymous figure in a chair adjacent to a red figure brandishing a gun. The scene displays the violence of the environment, in both palette and composition. We are forced to examine our conscience, and question the legitimacy of this treatment.

description_block:
Peter Clarke (South African, 1929-2014)
Cockstand 
signed and dated 'Clarke/ 31.5.1975' (lower right)
watercolour on paper 
62 x 46.5cm (24 7/16 x 18 5/16in).

Provenance
Acquired from the artist by Rashid Lombard; 
Sold at Strauss & Co, 2016;
A private collection.

Exhibited
Johannesburg, Standard Bank Gallery, 'Listening to Distant Thunder: The Art of Peter Clarke', (May-July 2011);
Cape Town, Iziko South African National Gallery, 'Listening to Distant Thunder: The Art of Peter Clarke', (October 2011-February 2012).

Literature
Philippa Hobbs and Elizabeth Rankin, Listening to Distant Thunder: The Art of Peter Clarke, (Johannesburg: Standard Bank of South Africa, 2011), p. 196. (illustrated). 

Two decades prior to the present works completion, Clarke had decided to fully commit himself to his career as an artist, quitting his job in the Simon's Town docks. This leap of faith showed fruitful as in 1955, three years later, he had won the Drum International Short Story Award, ahead of writers who would later become canonical figures, including Richard Rive and Cyprian Ekwensi. Clarke also attended the renowned University of Iowa Writers' Workshop in the United States.

This work was previously owned by South African political photo-journalist and founder of the Cape Town International Jazz Festival, Rashid Lombard. Peter Clarke had founded The Vakalisa Art Association in 1982 alongside writer and publisher James Matthews. This was a prominent network of black artists based in the Western Cape of South Africa. This association held cultural events and exhibitions in publicly accessible places such as libraries and community centres. Lombard was a member of this organisation alongside other artists such as Patrick Holo and Michael Barry.

With title and composition working in tandem, humour is an element of many of Clarke's works; 'a smug rooster perched on the buttocks of a man whose arched body takes up an absurd acrobatic pose, while a supine snake slithers below'(p. 196). The present work is indicative of Clark's daring nature of his practise which did not solely focus on the aesthetics of painting but incorporated wordplay and poetry, evidently important elements to the artist and his contemporaries.

Aphumelela

Provenance

Possibly linked to the isiXhosa word 'Phumelela', Aphumelela, meaning to achieve and prosper, aligns with the mood that the present work evokes. Large, closely cropped, and vivid, Aphumelela shares the intensity of Zanele Muholi's famous photographic work. Here, given the artists extension into painting, Muholi explores the malleability and surreal forms of expression that painting permits.

As a visual activist, championing black and LGBTQIA+ lives and voices, key themes of the artist's life and work embody power, reclaim, and presence. This is clearly supported in Muholi's artistic and business life, founding the Inkanyiso media forum and creating dynamic works of art championing the existence of their community.

The present work was created in the same year as the artists first ground braking solo show at the Tate Modern in London. The following year, they opened the Muholi Art Institute in Cape Town which aimed to support upcoming visual artists from South Africa. The ethos that the present work embodies is reflective of Muholi's activism, mentorship, and resistance against erasure.

Ouattara Watts (Ivory Coast, born 1957)
Matrix 00d 
signed, dated and titled (verso)
acrylic, oil and oilstick on canvas
200 x 260cm (78 3/4 x 102 3/8in).
(unframed)

Provenance

LIQUIDAZIONE GIUDIZIALE BIOERA S.P.A;
A private collection, Italy.

Exhibited
Rome, Magazzino d'Arte Moderna, Ouattara Watts: Outlaw, 16 December 2008–31 January 2009.
Milan, FM Centro per l'Arte Contemporanea, Frigoriferi Milanesi, Il Cacciatore Bianco / The White Hunter, 30 March–3 June 2017.

Monumental in scale and rich in symbolic complexity, Matrix 00d is a compelling example of Ouattara Watts's distinctive visual language. Across its expansive surface, numbers, signs, geometric forms, and vivid colours coexist within a composition that appears at once carefully structured and instinctive.

Born in Ivory Coast and educated in Paris, Watts moved to New York in 1988 upon the encouragement of Jean-Michel Basquiat, with whom he formed an immediate artistic friendship. Yet, Watts would forge a trajectory entirely his own, continuously resisting confinement to a single geography or cultural tradition. His paintings instead inhabit what the artist has described as a vision "beyond geography", drawing freely upon West African cosmologies, mathematics, spirituality, music and abstraction. Indeed, his international recognition culminated in his participation in both 'Documenta 11' and the Whitney Biennial in 2002, as well as also presenting at the Venice Biennale in 1993.

The title Matrix itself suggests an underlying structure: a space from which forms, ideas and relationships can emerge. Numbers and enigmatic signs punctuate the composition, while layers of colour and gesture give the painting an almost musical rhythm.

Immersive and enigmatic, Matrix 00d transforms the canvas into a field of connections. A space in which different histories, symbols and ways of understanding the world converge into a singular cosmology.

Literature

Quoted from a interview with Joost Bosland in relation to his exhibition at Michael Stevenson Gallery in 2008, Odili Donald Odita describes how visiting West Africa for Festac'77 and regular trips to Nigeria (living and working in Pennsylvania) have effected his colour sensibility:

"It has allowed me to relax my sense of colour association, to be less restrictive about what colours go together. I would see colour combinations in some of those textiles that I would never have thought of. Why couldn't I allow myself the same freedom? I also learned about the nature of dust, how it covers things, but also about how some powerful colours can penetrate a dusty space. I remember a visit to my aunt's house in the village. In my memory, everything was very dark, but when I had the pictures developed I was shocked by the intense blue of the wall, and the colour of their couch." ( Odili Donald Odita in Odili Donald Odita: Double Edge, ed. Sophie Perryer, (Michael Stevenson, 2008), p. 9.).

Prior to his solo show at Michael Stevenson, Odita was the recipient of the Penny McCall Foundation (1994), Joan Mitchell Foundation (2001), and Louis Comfort Tiffany(2007) grants. His 2007 installation Give me shelter was also featured in the 52nd Venice Biennale exhibition 'Think With The Senses, Feel With the Mind', curated by Robert Storr.

description_block:
Edoardo Villa (South African, 1915-2011)
Brusso (1993) 
painted steel 
235 x 40 x 45cm (92 1/2 x 15 3/4 x 17 11/16in).

Provenance
Acquired from Strauss & Co, June 2014;
A private collection.

Completed in 1993, the present work is the eighth of nine editions designed by Edoardo Villa. Similarly scaled works by the artist are currently held in NIROX sculpture park on loan from the Eduardo Villa Trust and the Villa-Legodi Centre for Sculpture dedicated to perpetuating the artists legacy.

Born in Bergamo of the Lombardy region in Italy where he studied at the studied at the Andrea Fontini Art School Villa moved to South Africa after being held there as a WWII prisoner of war following the Battle of Sidi Barrani in 1940. After his release in 1944, Villa remained in South Africa where he continued his vocation as a sculptor, beginning with traditional busts before developing into a cubist sensibility reminiscent of Pablo Picasso. In the 1950's, he secured a job teaching at the Polly Art Centre in Johannesburg, at the time on of the only exhibition centres that allowed black artists to display their works. He represented South Africa at the Venice Biennale five times, and the University of Pretoria opened an Edoardo Villa Museum in 1995.

Prior to Brusso's formation, in 1970 the Eduardo Villa Museum hosted a ground-breaking exhibition of seventy steel works by Villa across both its galleries and surrounding park. The show was a great success and was later transferred to the Johannesburg Art Gallery and Joubert Park.

Synthesising his European heritage with African sculptural influences, Villa's minimalistic structures explore the human form. During his residency at the Standard Bank Festival of the Arts in Grahamstown, Villa addressed his preoccupation within his work of this subject matter: "If anything could sum up my fundamental concern in art, it is that of the human and the individual – the human condition." (Edoardo Villa (1988), extract from Sean O'Toole (Villa-Legodi Centre for Sculpture, Online, 2016)).

The Saxophonist 
watercolour and pencil on wove paper

Provenance

Bonhams sale, New York, September 2020, Lot 10;
A private collection, US.

Nina Bergman was Dumile's partner and was with the artist in 1991 when he died of an heart-attack in Tower Records, 66th St, NYC. She wrote a moving account of his death:

"He wants to stop at Tower Records at 66th Street. We enter, walk to the Ray Charles he wants. I turn to ask him which cut he wants. He grabs my shoulders and falls to the floor.

He stops breathing. I cannot hear his heartbeat. I scream for help as I lunge on his chest beating the life back into him. His eyes open. He climbs back up the CD rack. The girl at the checkout won't hang up with her boyfriend to call the paramedics. Dumi drops to the floor again. His heartbeat stops. Dumi my companion of two years is gone."

It is characteristic of Dumile that his final moments were spent searching out a Ray Charles's CD, as his one great passion was for jazz music. He designed the cover art for a record produced by Hugh Masekela, with the two often talked together of their shared home:

"His art was about the suffering of our people. That suffering was a very deep scar in his life. I found him to have been like Frantz Fanon in his understanding of what was happening in South Africa."

Masekela also recalls the artist's warmth of character, how Dumile always used the few pennies he had to come and see him perform, and how, far from being a 'damné de la terre', he had a great sense of humour "He was not a depressed person, he was always looking for a laugh."

Perspective explores the strange irony of arriving at happiness without realising you are already there. The bright sky, flowers, colour and beauty create an almost perfect paradise, yet the goldfish seem completely unaware of it.

The goldfish become a humorous but poignant reflection of human nature. Like them, we spend our lives searching for happiness and waiting for the "perfect" moment, only to become so focused on what comes next that we forget to appreciate where we are.

There is also an irony that echoes Shelley's Ozymandias. While he desperately wanted to be remembered forever, time eventually erased almost everything. The goldfish are the opposite: they have everything worth remembering but cannot remember it. Somewhere between the two is where we sit.

The misspelled "Persp9ctivE" reinforces the idea that our perspective and memory are imperfect. Ultimately, the artwork reminds us that happiness may not be somewhere ahead of us. It is having the perspective to recognise when you've already arrived.

description_block:
Maud Frances Eyston Sumner (South African, 1902-1985)
Winter in Paris 
signed 'Sumner' (lower left)
oil on canvas 
53 x 64cm (20 7/8 x 25 3/16in).

Provenance
A private collection.

Beginning her Oxford education in 1922, and later at the Westminster School of Art and Académie de la Grande Chaumière in Paris, Maud Sumner spent most of her career in Europe. It was here that her creativity was formatively moulded, influenced by artists such as Edouard Vuillard (1868-1940) and Pierre Bonnard (1867-1947). Continuing to work in naturalist painting throughout the 1930s until the 1940s, Sumner was then exposed to the Rayonist movement, encouraging her own experiments with fragmentation and abstraction after the Second World War.

The present work is indicative of the paintings she was producing in the early 1930s. Winter in Paris encapsulates her preference for closely cropped domestic interiors with a bright palette. As an ever-present element of this era of work, despite the winter exterior, a vase of flowers sits on the desk in a palette that intertwines the sitter with the scene. The intimacy of the scene paired with the intimacy of the composition suggests a close relationship between the artist and the sitter.

Differing from many of Sumner's interior paintings, the present work also incorporates a view of an exterior scene through the two windows that dominate the picture. Exterior and interior scenes were regularly separate subject matters for the artist. Moreover, snow scenes, such as is present in Winter in Paris, were completed more regularly in watercolours such as Snow, Wappenbury (1939) and Snow, Eathorpe (1931). This rare fusion of the interior and exterior is a splendid demonstration of Sumner's ability to convey light and perspective. Sumner's holidays, and Christmases in particular, were spent at Eathorpe Park in Warwickshire, where her father had been married and her grandmother and aunts still lived, which was very much her second home until it was sold in the 1950s. Other 1930s studies of Eathorpe under snow can be found in the collections of Iziko South African National Gallery in Cape Town, the Johannesburg Art Gallery, the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford, and the Municipal Art Gallery in The Hague.

"This period of nearly a decade, from 1931 to the autumn of 1939, is a most important one in Maud Sumner's development and progress as a painter. It was a period, firstly, of consolidation: a crowded and exciting lustrum had passed since she settled in Paris, and the schools she had attended had done their work. She had now found her direction, and her affinity for Cézanne, for Vuillard and for Bonnard had given a firm base to her painting in oils. It was also the period of her most confident progress as an oil painter; and finally, during those years she reached the highest achievement of what might be called, conveniently as well as accurately, the first phrase of her development as a painter."(C. Eglington, p.14)
